title: LLD versus HLD interviews
idea: High-level design (HLD) chooses the services, data stores and network links of a system; low-level design (LLD) designs the classes and methods inside one service.
points: HLD asks which boxes exist and how they scale; LLD asks what classes do.
The same product gets both: HLD draws the shortener service, LLD writes its classes.
An LLD round runs: clarify, list entities, define contracts, code the core, then extend.
Interviewers score clear responsibilities, sound contracts and how cheaply your design absorbs follow-ups.

hero.title: One LLD round, start to finish

messages.label: Design a URL shortener's classes
messages.note: The prompt is vague on purpose. Treat it as an invitation to ask questions.

messages.label: Custom aliases? Expiry? Single process?
messages.note: Clarify scope first. Write the agreed use cases where the interviewer can see them.

messages.label: Shorten and resolve only, for now
messages.note: Now you know what is in scope and what will likely come later.

messages.label: ShortenerService, CodeGenerator, UrlRepository
messages.note: Name entities and contracts before code. Say why each interface exists.

messages.label: Code the core use case
messages.note: Write the main path end to end, with validation. Skip getters and boilerplate.

messages.label: Add custom aliases
messages.note: The follow-up tests your design. A good one bends in one place.

messages.label: saveIfAbsent + AliasTakenException
messages.note: Extend the contract, add one method, fail loudly on conflicts.

messages.label: Two users take one alias at once?
messages.note: Close with trade-offs: thread-safety, what you would test, what you left out.

code.title: The core round
code.caption: The LLD answer for shorten and resolve: two contracts and one service that depends only on them.

walk.text: Two interfaces mark the parts most likely to change: code generation and storage.
A base-36 counter is short and collision-free. Say aloud that it is not thread-safe.
The service receives both collaborators through its constructor and rejects nulls at once.
`shorten` validates first, then generates and saves. Bad input never reaches storage.
An unknown code returns an empty `Optional`, not null. The caller must decide what to show.
A non-web URL fails with `IllegalArgumentException`: a caller bug, so unchecked fits.

code.title: The follow-up
code.caption: The interviewer adds custom aliases. Only the new path is shown; the contract grows by one method.

walk.text: Saving now reports whether the code was free. Check and write are one call.
`putIfAbsent` on `ConcurrentHashMap` is atomic, which answers the closing concurrency question.
A taken alias gets its own named exception, so callers can catch exactly that case and offer another.
`shortenAs` validates the alias format, then lets storage decide if it is free.
The second claim on `q3` is refused, and the first mapping is untouched.

pitfalls: Drawing load balancers and databases in an LLD round; the interviewer wanted classes and methods.
Coding before agreeing scope; you build features nobody asked for and run out of time.
Checking then saving in two calls; under concurrency two users both win the same alias.

quiz.q: Which question belongs in an LLD round rather than an HLD round?
options: How many cache nodes will serve resolve traffic?
Which class decides that an alias is already taken?
Should the database be replicated across regions?
Where does the load balancer route a request?
quiz.why: LLD assigns responsibilities to classes inside one service. Cache nodes, replication and load balancers are infrastructure choices, which HLD makes.

takeaway: HLD picks the boxes; LLD designs the classes inside one box.
